```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 5,
  dpi = 96,
  dev = "jpeg",
  dev.args = list(quality = 90),
  out.width = "100%"
)
imgt_dir <- path.expand(Sys.getenv("SIRUP_IMGT_DIR"))
has_trees <- nzchar(imgt_dir) && dir.exists(imgt_dir)
```

<div markdown="1" style="background: #F7E5BC; padding: 12px; margin-bottom: 24px; line-height: 24px;">
  <p style="margin: -12px -12px 12px; padding: 6px 12px; background: #d6b676; color: #ffffff; font-weight: 700;"> <b>Note</b> </p>
  **Time:** ~25 minutes.<br>
  **Data:** two MG thymus sections, bulk thymus BCR-seq, and bulk blood BCR-seq, downloaded with `downloadSIRUPExample()`.<br>
  **Needs:** SIRUP, scoper, and dowser. The tree step also needs the IMGT reference sequences.
</div>

Most studies have more than one tissue section. You can also have bulk AIRR-seq of the same tissue, or blood from other time points. In this page, you put all of these samples in one SIRUP object. You call clones on all samples together. You then ask where each clone was seen, compare clonal dominance in each section, and build a lineage tree that has blood tips.

A clone is a group of B or T cells that descend from one ancestor cell and share its receptor rearrangement. If you call clones on all samples together, one clone ID names the same lineage in every sample.

One SIRUP object can hold all of this:

* `spatial` can be a named list of Seurat objects, one for each section.
* The receptor table holds the rows from every section and every bulk sample. A `sample` column tells SIRUP which sample each row belongs to.
* Rows whose `sample` does not name a section stay in the table as nonspatial rows. SIRUP does not put them on a tissue. Clone calling, trees, and your own summaries can use them.

This page follows Figure 5 of the SIRUP paper. The MG thymus data come from a patient who had a thymectomy. Besides the two Visium sections, there is bulk BCR-seq of the thymus. There is also bulk BCR-seq of blood, taken at the thymectomy and 12 months later. The question is which clones in ectopic germinal centers (eGCs) also appear in the blood. An eGC is a site in the thymus where B cells proliferate and mutate their receptors.

## Get the example data

This page uses example files that are not part of the SIRUP package. This code
downloads them. Change `dest` to a folder you want to keep. The default folder
is temporary. The function skips files that are already there.

```{r download-data}
extdata <- SIRUP::downloadSIRUPExample(
  dest = file.path(tempdir(), "SIRUP_example"),
  files = c(
  "mg_thymus_slice1_spatial.rds",
  "mg_thymus_slice2_spatial.rds",
  "mg_thymus_slice1_bcr.tsv.gz",
  "mg_thymus_slice2_bcr.tsv.gz",
  "mg_thymus_slice1_gc_polygons.csv",
  "mg_thymus_slice2_gc_polygons.csv",
  "mg_thymus_bulk_thymus_1.tsv.gz",
  "mg_thymus_bulk_thymus_2.tsv.gz",
  "mg_thymus_bulk_blood_month0_1.tsv.gz",
  "mg_thymus_bulk_blood_month0_2.tsv.gz",
  "mg_thymus_bulk_blood_month12_1.tsv.gz",
  "mg_thymus_bulk_blood_month12_2.tsv.gz"
  )
)
```

## Load the samples

```{r libraries, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(SIRUP)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

```{r load}
spatial <- list(
  mg_thymus_slice1 = readRDS(file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice1_spatial.rds")),
  mg_thymus_slice2 = readRDS(file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice2_spatial.rds"))
)

read_bcrs <- function(file, sample, compartment) {
  airr::read_rearrangement(file.path(extdata, file)) %>%
    mutate(sample = sample, compartment = compartment)
}

sections <- bind_rows(
  read_bcrs("mg_thymus_slice1_bcr.tsv.gz", "mg_thymus_slice1", "thymus_slice1"),
  read_bcrs("mg_thymus_slice2_bcr.tsv.gz", "mg_thymus_slice2", "thymus_slice2")
) %>%
  extractSpatialIds(
    id = "sequence_id",
    spatial_id = "barcode_10x",
    regex = ",([ACGT]{16})$",
    suffix = "-1"
  )

bulk <- bind_rows(
  read_bcrs("mg_thymus_bulk_thymus_1.tsv.gz", "bulk_thymus_1", "bulk_thymus"),
  read_bcrs("mg_thymus_bulk_thymus_2.tsv.gz", "bulk_thymus_2", "bulk_thymus"),
  read_bcrs("mg_thymus_bulk_blood_month0_1.tsv.gz", "bulk_blood_month0_1", "blood_month0"),
  read_bcrs("mg_thymus_bulk_blood_month0_2.tsv.gz", "bulk_blood_month0_2", "blood_month0"),
  read_bcrs("mg_thymus_bulk_blood_month12_1.tsv.gz", "bulk_blood_month12_1", "blood_month12"),
  read_bcrs("mg_thymus_bulk_blood_month12_2.tsv.gz", "bulk_blood_month12_2", "blood_month12")
)

bcrs <- bind_rows(sections, bulk) %>%
  mutate(sequence_id = paste(sample, gsub(",", "_", sequence_id), sep = "_")) %>%
  filterAirr(
    locus_val = "IGH",
    min_v_length = 250,
    min_j_length = 30,
    min_junction_length = 10,
    productive_only = TRUE,
    min_consensus_count = NULL
  ) %>%
  filter(!grepl("[^ACGT]", junction))

count(bcrs, compartment, sample)
```

`read_bcrs()` reads one AIRR file and adds two columns: `sample` and `compartment`. After the barcodes come out of the section IDs, the code makes each `sequence_id` unique and safe for trees. It puts the sample name in front, because IDs repeat between files. It replaces the comma with `_`, because dowser renames tree tips that contain a comma.

The section rows get a `sample` that matches the names of the `spatial` list. The bulk and blood rows have their own sample names and no barcode.

<div markdown="1" style="background: #F7E5BC; padding: 12px; margin-bottom: 24px; line-height: 24px;">
  <p style="margin: -12px -12px 12px; padding: 6px 12px; background: #d6b676; color: #ffffff; font-weight: 700;"> <b>Note</b> </p>
  To keep the package small, the bulk files hold a subset of the bulk data. They hold the blood sequences of clones seen in a section. They also hold up to 10 bulk thymus sequences of each clone that reaches the blood.
</div>

## Create a multi-sample object

Give `createSIRUP()` the named list. Give the name of the `sample` column to `sample_id`.

```{r create}
sirup <- createSIRUP(
  spatial = spatial,
  receptors = bcrs,
  spatial_id = "barcode_10x",
  sample_id = "sample",
  image_scale = "lowres",
  swap_coords = FALSE
)

sirup
spatialSamples(sirup)
```

Visium barcodes repeat between sections. For example, `AAACAAGTATCTCCCA-1` exists in both. SIRUP matches each receptor to a spot by the pair of sample and barcode, so the two sections never mix. A spot is one capture area of the Visium slide.

If the sections need different image settings, give named values: `image_scale = c(mg_thymus_slice1 = "hires", mg_thymus_slice2 = "lowres")`.

## Get one sample

The accessors take a `sample_id` argument.

```{r accessors}
getSpatial(sirup, "mg_thymus_slice1")
nrow(getReceptors(sirup, "mg_thymus_slice1"))
nrow(getReceptors(sirup))
```

`filterSample()` returns a new SIRUP object with one section. It drops the nonspatial rows.

```{r filter-sample}
slice1 <- filterSample(sirup, "mg_thymus_slice1")
slice1
```

`subsetSIRUP()` gives finer control. It can keep a set of spots or a set of receptor rows. With `keep_nonspatial_receptors = TRUE`, it also keeps the bulk rows.

`mergeSIRUP()` goes the other way. It combines single-section objects into a multi-sample object, and it adds a sample column with the names that you give.

```{r merge}
slice2 <- filterSample(sirup, "mg_thymus_slice2")
merged <- mergeSIRUP(
  slice1, slice2,
  samples = c("mg_thymus_slice1", "mg_thymus_slice2"),
  sample_field = "sample"
)
merged
```

## Add polygons for each section

A polygon is a closed outline that selects the spots of one tissue region. Give `addPolygons()` a named vector of polygon files, one for each section.

```{r polygons}
sirup <- addPolygons(sirup, polygons_path = c(
  mg_thymus_slice1 = file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice1_gc_polygons.csv"),
  mg_thymus_slice2 = file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice2_gc_polygons.csv")
))

getPolygons(sirup)
```

Both files number their eGCs from 1. SIRUP adds the sample to each polygon ID. `mg_thymus_slice1::1` and `mg_thymus_slice2::1` are different regions.

## Plot several sections

A spatial plot of a multi-sample object returns a list with one plot for each section. Set `combine_sample_plots = TRUE` to get one combined figure. Give `sample_id` to plot one section.

```{r plots, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 4.5}
plotSpatialPolygons(sirup, zoom = TRUE, combine_sample_plots = TRUE)
```

```{r plot-one}
spatialExpressionPlot(
  sirup,
  features = "AICDA",
  assay = "alra",
  layer = "data",
  sample_id = "mg_thymus_slice1",
  title = "AICDA, section 1"
)
```

## Call clones across all samples

Call clones on the whole receptor table. One clone ID then covers the sections, the bulk thymus, and the blood.

```{r clones, message = FALSE}
sirup <- updateReceptors(
  sirup,
  scoper::hierarchicalClones,
  threshold = 0.1,
  summarize_clones = FALSE,
  nproc = 1
)
dplyr::n_distinct(getReceptors(sirup)$clone_id)
```

## Find where each clone was seen

Each row has a `compartment`. For each clone, the code below counts the sequences in each compartment. It also records the eGCs that hold the clone.

```{r presence}
clones <- getReceptors(sirup) %>%
  group_by(clone_id) %>%
  summarise(
    in_section = any(compartment %in% c("thymus_slice1", "thymus_slice2")),
    n_egc = sum(!is.na(polygon_id)),
    egcs = paste(sort(unique(na.omit(polygon_id))), collapse = ", "),
    n_bulk_thymus = sum(compartment == "bulk_thymus"),
    n_blood_month0 = sum(compartment == "blood_month0"),
    n_blood_month12 = sum(compartment == "blood_month12")
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    in_egc = n_egc > 0,
    in_blood = n_blood_month0 + n_blood_month12 > 0
  )

count(clones, in_egc, in_blood)
```

The table shows that most clones stay in the thymus. A few eGC clones also appear in the blood. The SIRUP paper calls these clones exported. Fisher's exact test compares the eGC clones with the other clones of the sections.

```{r fisher}
section_clones <- filter(clones, in_section)
fisher.test(table(section_clones$in_egc, section_clones$in_blood))
```

For each eGC, count the clones that it holds and the clones that reach the blood.

```{r per-egc}
getReceptors(sirup) %>%
  filter(!is.na(polygon_id)) %>%
  distinct(polygon_id, clone_id) %>%
  left_join(select(clones, clone_id, in_blood), by = "clone_id") %>%
  group_by(polygon_id) %>%
  summarise(n_clones = n(), n_exported = sum(in_blood)) %>%
  arrange(desc(n_exported))
```

The bulk files hold a subset of the bulk data, and the clones come from that subset. For the full analysis, see Figure 5 of the SIRUP paper.

## Measure clonal dominance in each section

Clonal dominance is the share of the receptors in a region that belong to its largest clones. The regional functions work on all sections at once. The dominance table has a `sample` column and the full `polygon_id`. For a longer treatment, see `vignette("regions", package = "SIRUP")`.

```{r dominance}
dominance <- spatialCloneDominance(object = sirup, locus_val = "IGH")

dominance$dominance %>%
  group_by(polygon_id) %>%
  slice_max(proportion, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(sample, polygon_id, clone_id, n_receptors, proportion) %>%
  head()
```

Most plotting functions return a named list with one plot for each section.

```{r region-receptors}
region_plots <- plotSpatialRegionReceptors(
  dominance = dominance,
  object = sirup,
  top_n = 8,
  point_size = 1.5,
  zoom = TRUE
)
names(region_plots)
region_plots$mg_thymus_slice1
```

`plotSpatialPolygonPies()` also works on all sections at once. Give `sample_id` to draw the pies of one section next to its map.

```{r pies, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 6}
pies <- plotSpatialPolygonPies(
  dominance = dominance,
  object = sirup,
  fill = "clone_id",
  top_n = 5,
  sample_id = "mg_thymus_slice1"
)
pies$page_1
```

## Build a tree with blood tips

A lineage tree shows how the sequences of one clone relate to each other. Each tip of the tree is one sequence. A tree can mix spatial and bulk sequences. The code below picks an exported eGC clone with blood sequences from both time points.

```{r pick-clone}
exported <- clones %>%
  filter(in_egc, n_blood_month0 > 0, n_blood_month12 > 0) %>%
  mutate(n_total = n_egc + n_bulk_thymus + n_blood_month0 + n_blood_month12) %>%
  filter(n_total <= 100) %>%
  arrange(desc(n_blood_month0 + n_blood_month12))
exported

tree_clone <- exported$clone_id[[1]]
tree_section <- sub("::.*$", "", exported$egcs[[1]])
tree_section
```

Make the germline of the clone with `dowser::createGermlines()`. The germline is the sequence of the unmutated ancestor, and the tree starts there. Then build the tree. As in `vignette("clones-and-trees", package = "SIRUP")`, the germline step needs the IMGT reference sequences. Set the environment variable `SIRUP_IMGT_DIR` to the folder that holds them. The tree chunks run only when that folder exists.

Keep `compartment` in `traits`. The tree plot uses it to set the tip shapes.

```{r tree, eval = has_trees}
tree_sirup <- updateReceptors(sirup, dplyr::filter, clone_id == tree_clone)
tree_sirup <- updateReceptors(
  tree_sirup,
  dowser::createGermlines,
  references = dowser::readIMGT(imgt_dir),
  id = "sequence_id"
)
tree_sirup <- formatSpatialClones(
  tree_sirup,
  id = "sequence_id",
  traits = c("barcode_10x", "sample", "compartment", "polygon_id")
)
set.seed(1)
tree_sirup <- getSpatialTrees(tree_sirup)
trees <- getAnalysis(tree_sirup, "trees")
```

`plotSpatialCloneTreePairs()` puts the spatial tips on their sections. Bulk and blood tips appear in the tree only. The argument `shape_by` sets one shape for each compartment. The argument `color_by` colors the tips by tree cluster. `clusterTreesTips()` makes the clusters.

```{r tree-plot, eval = has_trees, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 6}
trees <- clusterTreesTips(trees, k = "auto", id = "sequence_id", k_range = 1:6)

pair <- plotSpatialCloneTreePairs(
  trees,
  object = sirup,
  id = "sequence_id",
  color_by = "tree_cluster",
  shape_by = "compartment",
  shape_values = c(
    thymus_slice1 = 21, thymus_slice2 = 21, bulk_thymus = 22,
    blood_month0 = 24, blood_month12 = 23
  ),
  zoom = TRUE,
  polygons = TRUE,
  polygon_alpha = 0,
  polygon_color = "black",
  show_spatial_legend = TRUE
)

names(pair)
```

The list has one element for each clone. If the tips of a clone fall in more than one section, the list has one element for each clone and section instead. These elements are named `<clone>::<sample>`. Each one pairs the full tree with the map of one section. Each element also holds a `legend` for the tip colors. The function builds it because the call sets `show_spatial_legend = TRUE`. The code below shows the section that holds the eGC tips.

```{r tree-plot-show, eval = has_trees, fig.width = 14, fig.height = 7}
key <- paste0(tree_clone, "::", tree_section)
if (!key %in% names(pair)) key <- tree_clone
section_pair <- pair[[key]]

cowplot::plot_grid(
  cowplot::plot_grid(section_pair$tree, section_pair$spatial_clone, rel_widths = c(1.3, 1)),
  section_pair$legend,
  ncol = 1,
  rel_heights = c(1, section_pair$legend_rel_height)
)
```

Shapes show the compartment of each tip. Circles are tips from a section. Squares are bulk thymus. Triangles are blood at the thymectomy. Diamonds are blood 12 months later. The legend shows the colors, which are the tree clusters from `clusterTreesTips()`. On the map, a dot has the color of its tip.

## Save the object

`saveSIRUP()` writes the whole object to one file. `readSIRUP()` reads it back and checks it.

```{r save}
path <- file.path(tempdir(), "mg_thymus.sirup.rds")
saveSIRUP(sirup, path)
readSIRUP(path)
```
